Section 1
The Guardian clarified that a new law making the abduction of a cat or dog a specific criminal offence has taken effect, but it applies only to England and Northern Ireland, not the whole UK. It also corrected its reference to Eileen Burbidge, noting she is the executive director of Fertifa while the company’s founders are Tony Chen and Nick Kuan. Additionally, the paper amended an interview with actor Juliet Stevenson, stating she worked with director Alex Lawther, not “Lowther,” and clarified that the family at the heart of Bend It Like Beckham is Sikh, not Muslim.

Section 2
The Guardian also amended its story about Venetia Stanley’s relationship with early‑20th‑century prime minister Herbert Asquith, explaining that it was her uncle, the third Baron Stanley of Alderley, who converted to Islam, not her father, the fourth Baron Stanley. These revisions appear in the August 25 editions on pages 16, 53, 7 and 3 respectively.

***
Section 3
Other recently amended articles include: Telegram app founder Pavel Durov reportedly arrested at French airport; From ratcatcher to keeper of the snow: royal servants enter the spotlight in new exhibitions; ‘It’s about getting the job done’: Pope happy with England’s cautious chase; Britain could be a sci‑tech superpower – if the Treasury stopped holding it back; Salvator Mundi, Saudi Arabia and the saga of the missing masterpiece; Last of the summer wines. * The article about the Telegram founder’s arrest was updated with new details from French authorities. * The piece on royal servants now includes additional photographs from the exhibition.

Section 4
Readers wishing to contact the Readers’ Editor can write to the Observer at York Way, London N1 9GU, email observer.readers@observer.co.uk, or telephone 020 3353 4736.
